V02-B-001: Projects that recruit volunteers to count birds, record flowering dates or photograph insects are often dismissed by professional researchers on the grounds that amateurs make mistakes. The objection is true and largely beside the point. Individual records from volunteers are indeed less reliable than those of trained surveyors, but the errors tend to be random rather than systematic, and random errors shrink in importance as the number of observations grows. A thousand imperfect counts spread across a region can reveal a trend that a handful of expert surveys, confined to a few accessible sites, would miss altogether. The real weakness of such data lies elsewhere: volunteers go where it is pleasant to go, at weekends and in good weather, so the gaps in their coverage are anything but random. The question to ask of citizen science is therefore not how careful each participant is but where and when the participants chose to look.
V02-B-002: Advocates of rewilding sometimes speak as though removing fences and reintroducing a few large animals will return a landscape to the condition it was in before human interference. The promise is appealing but confused. There is no single earlier condition to return to: the landscapes in question have changed continuously for thousands of years, with shifts in climate, in the species present and in the ways people used them. Choosing a baseline is therefore a decision about which past to prefer, not a discovery of the true one. This does not make rewilding pointless. Letting natural processes such as flooding, grazing and decay operate with less management can produce richer and more resilient ecosystems. But the honest case for it is about the processes it allows, not about a lost original it claims to restore.
V02-B-003: An offset that pays to plant a forest is often treated as cancelling an equivalent quantity of emissions from a flight or a factory. The equivalence is only arithmetical. Carbon released from burning fossil fuel stays in the atmosphere for centuries, while carbon stored in trees is held only as long as the trees survive fire, disease, drought and the decisions of future landowners. The two quantities are measured in the same tonnes, yet one is a near-permanent addition and the other a reversible loan. None of this means that planting forests is worthless; a stored tonne buys time, and time has value. It means that an offset should be counted as a delay whose worth depends on how securely the storage can be guaranteed, rather than as an erasure that lets the original emission be forgotten.
V02-B-004: Much of what biologists know about how genes, cells and nervous systems work comes from a small number of species: a fruit fly, a roundworm, a small weed of the mustard family, the laboratory mouse. These organisms were not chosen because they are typical of life. They were chosen because they breed quickly, survive in captivity and can be manipulated easily, and once a community of researchers had built tools and stocks around them, each new study was cheaper to do in the same species than in a new one. The result is a body of knowledge that is deep but narrow, and whose generality is often assumed rather than tested. Findings that hold in a mouse may hold in people, and frequently do; but the reasons the mouse was studied had little to do with its resemblance to us.
V02-B-005: Writing tools that suggest the next word or complete a sentence are usually judged by whether their suggestions are accurate, that is, whether they offer what the writer was about to type. By that standard they are improving quickly. But accuracy measured this way rewards the most probable continuation, and the most probable continuation is, by definition, the one that most writers have already used. A tool that is perfectly accurate in this sense would steer each writer a little towards the common phrase and away from the unusual one, and across millions of documents these small nudges could make prose more uniform without anyone deciding that it should be. The danger lies not in any single suggestion, which the writer is free to refuse, but in the cumulative pull of accepting the easy option many times a day.
V02-B-006: Manufacturers who make devices hard to open, refuse to sell spare parts or tie components to software locks usually justify these choices on grounds of safety and quality. Some of the concern is genuine: a badly fitted battery can catch fire. Yet the same arguments were once made about cars, and an independent repair trade grew up around them without the roads becoming notably more dangerous. What restrictions on repair reliably achieve is not safety but control over the after-sales market, together with shorter lives for the products themselves. Where real hazards exist, they can be handled by setting standards for repairers rather than by excluding everyone but the original maker.
V02-B-007: It is often assumed that digital records, because they can be copied without loss, are safer than paper ones. A manuscript can burn; a file can be duplicated a thousand times. But a copy is only useful if something can still read it. Files depend on formats, formats on software, and software on machines and operating systems that are replaced every few years, so a perfectly preserved sequence of bits can become unreadable simply because the programs that understood it have gone. Paper asks nothing of its reader except literacy and light. Digital preservation is therefore less a matter of storing data than of continually maintaining the conditions under which data can be interpreted, a task that never finishes and is easy to neglect.
V02-B-008: Defenders of recommendation systems argue that they merely give people more of what they already like, and that this is a service rather than a manipulation. The claim assumes that preferences exist fully formed before the recommendations arrive. Taste, however, is partly made by exposure: people come to like music, food or films they have encountered repeatedly, and they rarely develop a liking for what they never meet. A system that learns from what someone has chosen, and then shows them more of the same, is therefore not simply reflecting a preference but helping to fix it, narrowing the range of encounters from which future preferences could grow. This need not be sinister, and the user remains free to search elsewhere. But it means the defence of such systems as neutral mirrors is mistaken.
V02-B-009: When a writer dies leaving a novel unfinished, or instructs that drafts be destroyed, those who hold the papers face a familiar dilemma. Publishing seems to betray the author's wishes or, at least, to present as a book what the author never judged to be one. Suppressing seems to deprive readers of work that may be among the best the writer produced. The dilemma is usually framed as loyalty against value, but this framing overlooks a third consideration: how the work is presented. An unfinished draft printed as a draft, with its gaps visible and its status made plain, misrepresents the author far less than the same text smoothed by an editor into the appearance of completion. The question is not only whether to publish but in what form.
V02-B-010: When a painting long admired as the work of a master is shown to be a forgery, its price collapses, and many viewers report that it now looks worse to them. Sceptics take this as proof that the art world values names rather than pictures, since the canvas itself has not changed. The inference is too quick. What we admire in a work is not only the arrangement of paint before us but also an achievement: a solution to a problem, reached at a certain time by a certain person. A forger who copies a style after it has been invented has not achieved what the original painter achieved, even if the surfaces are indistinguishable. Some of the lost esteem is snobbery, no doubt; but some of it tracks a real difference that the eye alone cannot see.
V02-B-011: The bare, white-walled gallery with even lighting and no decoration is often described as a neutral setting, one that lets the art speak for itself. It is better understood as a setting with very strong effects of its own. By removing every sign of daily life, it tells visitors that what hangs there is set apart, to be contemplated rather than used, touched or talked over. Objects that were made to be handled in a home, carried in a procession or worn on the body take on a different character when isolated on a plinth under a spotlight. The white room is not wrong for that reason, and for some works it may be ideal. But it is a choice that shapes what we see, and calling it neutral hides that choice from view.
V02-B-012: It is widely observed that a novel's sales rise sharply once it is shortlisted for a major literary prize, and rise again if it wins. This is often cited as evidence that prizes help good writing find readers. That is partly true, but the effect is concentrated. Because a shortlist directs attention to a handful of books rather than spreading it across hundreds, the gain for those chosen may come partly at the expense of comparable books that narrowly missed out, whose sales are not lifted at all. Prizes, in other words, may do less to enlarge the audience for serious fiction than to redistribute an existing audience towards a few titles.
V02-B-013: When a dictionary adds a slang term or records a new sense for an old word, complaints follow that it has abandoned standards. The complaint misunderstands what most modern dictionaries are for. They aim to record how a language is actually used, much as a map records where roads actually run, and a map that omitted a busy road because planners disapproved of it would simply be a bad map. Recording a usage is not endorsing it. Readers who want advice on what is appropriate in formal writing are entitled to it, and usage notes and style guides exist to provide it. The mistake lies in expecting one book to do both jobs and then blaming it for doing the one it set out to do.
V02-B-014: Newspaper headlines have long had a grammar of their own: articles and linking verbs drop out, short words such as 'bid', 'probe' and 'row' replace longer ones, and the present tense is used for events that are already over. These habits arose from a practical constraint, the need to fit a message into a narrow column in large type. They persist on screens, where space is less tight, partly because readers have learned to decode them and partly because brevity still helps a headline compete for attention. The cost is ambiguity: a compressed headline can sometimes be read in two ways, and the reader must open the story to find out which was meant.
V02-B-015: Schools that teach a standard form of a language are sometimes accused of destroying the regional dialects their pupils bring from home. The charge contains a truth: children who are told that their way of speaking is wrong often come to feel that it is, and may abandon it. But the fault lies in the telling, not in the teaching of the standard itself. Learning a second variety of one's language, useful in examinations, offices and correspondence with strangers, need not displace the first, any more than learning a second language erases one's mother tongue. Many speakers move between dialect and standard with ease, choosing according to company. What threatens a dialect is the attitude that treats it as a mistake, not the addition of another way of speaking.
V02-B-016: Listeners often describe a favourite podcast host as a friend, and the feeling is not hard to explain. Audio reaches us at close range, frequently through earphones, while we are alone and doing something else: driving, cooking, walking. The host's voice is unpolished and conversational, with hesitations and jokes that a scripted broadcast would remove, and it returns at regular intervals for hours each week. These conditions mimic the circumstances of real friendship closely enough that the mind responds as if to one. The relationship is, of course, one-sided: the host does not know the listener exists. That asymmetry is harmless for most people, but it is also what makes the medium so effective for advertising, since a recommendation from a 'friend' carries unusual weight.
V02-B-017: Studies of homework have tended to find that the amount of homework older pupils do is associated with higher achievement, while for young children the link is weak or absent. It is tempting to conclude that more homework simply works for teenagers. But an association of this kind can arise in several ways: pupils who are already motivated, or whose families support study, both do more homework and do better at school, so the homework may be partly a sign of advantage rather than its cause. And beyond a certain amount, the association often fades. The evidence supports homework that is moderate, purposeful and suited to the pupil's age, not the belief that more is always better.
V02-B-018: Complaints about grade inflation usually focus on fairness to earlier generations, whose hard-won marks now look ordinary beside the higher grades awarded today. The more serious cost falls elsewhere. A grade is useful to an employer or a university chiefly as a way of telling candidates apart, and when most candidates crowd into the top band, it stops doing that job. Selectors then fall back on other evidence, such as the standing of the institution, interviews, or the polish of a personal statement, which tend to favour candidates from privileged backgrounds more than marks did. Inflation that looks generous to every student can thus end up shifting advantage towards those who needed it least.
V02-B-019: Many teachers have been trained to identify each pupil's learning style, whether visual, auditory or kinaesthetic, and to match lessons to it. The idea is attractive because it seems to respect individual differences. Yet when it has been tested by teaching pupils in a style that matches their supposed preference and comparing them with pupils taught in a mismatched style, the expected advantage has generally failed to appear. People certainly have preferences about how they like to learn; what is doubtful is that those preferences determine how well they learn. More often, the best form of presentation depends on the material: maps are best shown and pronunciation is best heard, whoever the learner is.
V02-B-020: Memorisation has a poor reputation in modern education, where it is often set against understanding as the lower activity against the higher. The opposition is overdrawn. Understanding works on material held in mind: a pupil who must look up every multiplication fact or every date has little attention left for noticing patterns or weighing causes. Knowledge stored securely in memory is what frees thought to operate on something. None of this justifies drilling facts that are never connected to anything, which is as dull as its critics claim and is quickly forgotten. The case is for memory in the service of understanding, not memory in its place.
V02-B-021: Coaching for entrance examinations is criticised on two different grounds that are often run together. One is that it is unfair: families who can pay for it buy their children an advantage that others cannot. The other is that it defeats the purpose of the test, which was meant to measure ability, by inflating scores without improving the underlying skills. The two objections pull in different directions. If coaching genuinely builds skills, the second objection fails, but the first becomes stronger, since a real advantage is being bought. If coaching merely teaches tricks, the second objection holds, but the unfairness is less troubling, because the advantage it buys is partly illusory. Critics who press both at full strength at once owe an account of how coaching can be both useless and decisive.
V02-B-022: Some small trials have reported that patients given pills they are told openly contain no active ingredient nonetheless describe their symptoms as improved. The finding seems to dissolve the ethical objection to placebos, which rested on the need to deceive. It should be read with care. The improvements reported have mainly been in symptoms that patients assess themselves, such as pain or discomfort, rather than in measures of underlying disease, and in trials where patients cannot be blinded to what they received, expectations can colour reports. The pills may also work less through the pill than through the ritual around it: a consultation, an explanation, a doctor's attention. What the trials suggest is that care itself has effects, not that sugar does.
V02-B-023: Screening programmes are usually judged by how many cases of disease they find, and by that measure more sensitive tests always look better. But some conditions that screening detects would never have caused harm in a person's lifetime: small, slow-growing abnormalities that would have stayed silent until the person died of something else. Finding these is not a benefit; it converts healthy people into patients, exposing them to anxiety and to treatments with real side effects. Because no one can tell, in an individual case, whether a detected abnormality would have progressed, the overdiagnosed patient is indistinguishable from one whose life was saved, and may well believe that screening saved them. Counting detections therefore overstates what screening achieves, without implying that screening is never worthwhile.
V02-B-024: Every time an antibiotic is used, bacteria that happen to resist it gain an advantage over those that do not, so resistance spreads in proportion to use, including use that does the patient no good, as when antibiotics are taken for viral infections they cannot touch. This makes antibiotics unlike most medicines. A painkiller taken unnecessarily affects only the person who takes it; an antibiotic taken unnecessarily slightly reduces the usefulness of the drug for everyone. Decisions that look private, between one doctor and one patient, therefore have a shared cost. Treating antibiotics as a common resource, to be used when needed but not casually, is not excessive caution but a recognition of how they work.
V02-B-025: When patients fail to take medicines as prescribed, the problem is commonly described as one of forgetfulness or carelessness, and the proposed remedies are reminders: alarms, pill boxes, text messages. These help some people. But many patients who stop taking a drug have not forgotten it; they have decided, for reasons that seem good to them, such as side effects, cost, doubts about whether it works, or a regimen that clashes with their working day. Reminders do nothing for a patient who has chosen not to take a pill and may irritate one who has. Improving adherence therefore depends less on prompting patients than on finding out why they stop, which requires asking them.
